name: Interest evolution, shift, next-intent prediction, and proactive interest transition
venue_year: RepeatNet AAAI 2019; DIEN AAAI 2019; ISLF IJCAI 2019; Intention-Aware Sequential Recommendation TKDE 2022; CFPRec IJCAI 2022; Next Basket Recommendation Reality Check TOIS 2023; Sequential Recommendation with Distribution Shifts SIGIR 2023; NNBR SIGIR 2023; TGB-Seq ICLR 2025; Proactive Recommendation/T-PRA AI Open 2025; ProRec-Video AAAI 2026
official_sources: https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33014806 ; https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33015941 ; https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2019/799 ; https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2019/0799.pdf ; https://doi.org/10.1109/TKDE.2021.3050571 ; https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2022/521 ; https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2022/0521.pdf ; https://doi.org/10.1145/3587153 ; https://doi.org/10.1145/3539618.3591624 ; https://doi.org/10.1145/3604915.3608803 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.01308 ; https://openreview.net/forum?id=8e2LirwiJT ; https://github.com/TGB-Seq/TGB-Seq ; https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aiopen.2025.08.003 ; https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v40i17.38475
release_and_license: DIEN, ISLF, CFPRec, the distribution-shift paper, NNBR, and ProRec-Video have verified proceedings or publisher records; ISLF, CFPRec, and NNBR full texts were publicly accessible. DIEN evaluates public Amazon plus private Taobao advertising data, while its production logs are private. ISLF uses YOOCHOOSE and Diginetica under their original challenge terms. CFPRec uses three public check-in datasets, but redistribution and current download status must be checked separately [uncertain]. NNBR uses Ta-Feng, dunnhumby, and Instacart under separate terms. Public data/code for the 2025 proactive-causal paper and ProRec-Video were not verified [uncertain].
input_history: DIEN consumes a user's chronological behavior sequence plus a candidate target ad/item. ISLF consumes only the current anonymous session and models short-term, long-term, and latent factors. Intention-Aware Sequential Recommendation infers latent intents and structured transitions from an item sequence. CFPRec consumes historical check-in trajectories and context, then self-ensembles inferred multi-step future preferences. The distribution-shift framework uses historical interaction sequences under train/test distribution change. NNBR uses ordered prior purchase baskets. Proactive Recommendation and ProRec-Video use historical interests plus candidate transition content; ProRec-Video additionally profiles receptivity and adapts to simulated/dynamic feedback.
prediction_target: RepeatNet predicts the next session item through repeat versus explore modes; explore means choosing outside the current session, not a new category. DIEN predicts CTR for a supplied candidate item. ISLF and the structured-intent model rank the next item in a session/sequence. CFPRec predicts the next POI, not a semantic interest label or the actual multi-step future sequence. The NBR Reality Check evaluates next-basket items while decomposing repeat and explore. The distribution-shift work predicts future interactions under shifted item popularity/user preference distributions. NNBR predicts only items never consumed before in the next basket. TGB-Seq predicts future temporal graph destinations/edges under low repetition, not semantic interest. The 2025 proactive-causal T-PRA line aims to steer future interest through recommendation interventions [uncertain acronym expansion/details]. ProRec-Video plans a hierarchical semantic interest-transition path and corresponding video sequence, then reports transition success and satisfaction.
novel_interest_definition: DIEN, ISLF, structured-intent recommendation, and CFPRec do not operationalize a history-absent interest: 'interest' or 'intent' is an internal representation used for candidate CTR or next-item prediction. The distribution-shift framework studies changed future distributions, not first-ever semantic interests. NNBR defines novelty exactly as an item absent from every prior basket, but not a new category. Proactive Recommendation treats interest as causally steerable beyond current preferences [uncertain operational label]. ProRec-Video explicitly seeks content beyond historical preferences and plans transitions among hierarchical interest concepts, making it the closest semantic interest-shift work, but its ground-truth interest labels and persistence criterion are not public [uncertain].
novelty_granularity_and_reference_window: DIEN: none; target-item relevance is conditioned on sequence history. ISLF and structured-intent work: latent intent, with no observable novel category. CFPRec: next POI identity. Distribution-shift: population/item-preference distribution. NNBR: item-level novelty relative to all input baskets. ProRec-Video: hierarchical interest-node transition relative to historical preferences, but taxonomy and lookback window are [uncertain].
interest_onset_definition: DIEN uses a target-item click. ISLF and structured-intent models use the next click/item. CFPRec uses the next POI check-in. NNBR uses first observed purchase of an item in the next basket. ProRec-Video reports an interest-transition success rate and user satisfaction, but the primary record does not establish whether success means simulated acceptance, a click, sustained consumption, or another judge [uncertain]. None of the classical models requires repeat adoption of a new semantic interest.
is_direct_match: Direct at item granularity: NNBR. Direct/closest but not yet a public forecasting benchmark: ProRec-Video and the 2025 proactive-causal T-PRA line. Evaluation-framework adjacent: the NBR Reality Check. Robustness-only: sequential recommendation under distribution shifts and TGB-Seq. Adjacent next-location planning: CFPRec. Repeat/explore mechanism only: RepeatNet. Representation or candidate-ranking only, not novel-interest forecasting: DIEN, ISLF, and structured-intent sequential recommendation. Modeling an evolving hidden state is not the same as predicting an observed new interest.
persistence_signal: DIEN, ISLF, structured-intent recommendation, CFPRec, distribution-shift evaluation, and NNBR score immediate next-event outcomes without a later confirmation window. ProRec-Video adapts using ongoing feedback, which could support persistence auditing, but its published abstract reports transition success and satisfaction rather than repeated later adoption of each new interest [uncertain].
method: DIEN uses a GRU-based interest extractor with auxiliary next-behavior supervision and a target-aware interest-evolution layer. ISLF combines recurrent-VAE latent factors with long-/short-term session interest and attention. Structured-intent recommendation models discrete/latent intents and their transition structure before next-item ranking. CFPRec self-ensembles multi-step future-preference representations inferred from past periodic trajectories and fuses them with current preference. The SIGIR 2023 framework explicitly trains sequential recommenders for distribution shifts [uncertain implementation detail]. NNBR uses a bidirectional transformer with item/basket masking and swapping. The proactive-causal paper treats recommendations as interventions that steer interest [uncertain method detail]. ProRec-Video combines receptivity profiling, hierarchical transition planning, semantic video sequencing, agent-based simulation, Reflexion, and dynamic feedback adaptation.
evaluation_protocol: DIEN reports offline public/industrial CTR prediction and an online Taobao deployment result; it does not isolate novel categories. ISLF performs next-click sequence splitting on YOOCHOOSE-1/64, YOOCHOOSE-1/4, and Diginetica, removes length-one sessions and infrequent items, excludes test-only items, and reports Recall@20 and MRR@20. CFPRec evaluates next-POI HR and NDCG on three check-in datasets. The distribution-shift work evaluates future sequential recommendation under shifted popularity/preferences, not a first-onset label. NNBR uses five user-disjoint 80/20 splits with 10% of train users for validation and reports Recall/NDCG for next-basket novel items. ProRec-Video reports 85% interest-transition success and 78.3% user satisfaction on two datasets, but dataset identities, judging, candidates, and statistical protocol are [uncertain].
generalization_axis: DIEN: candidate CTR, including private online deployment, not user/category-disjoint. ISLF: later session events for anonymous sessions, with test items constrained to train vocabulary. Structured-intent work: seen-item next-item generalization. CFPRec: future check-in within existing POI vocabulary. Distribution-shift work: temporal/popularity/preference shift. NNBR: user-disjoint train/test but seen item vocabulary and item-level novelty. ProRec-Video: semantic transition beyond current preference [uncertain whether users, interest nodes, or items are held out].
exposure_handling: DIEN uses logged impressions/clicks for candidate CTR but does not publish propensities or randomized exposure. ISLF, structured-intent models, CFPRec, and NNBR use positive sequences without complete exposure sets. The distribution-shift paper addresses distribution change, not necessarily MNAR exposure. Proactive Recommendation is causal in framing [uncertain whether it has randomized or identified observational exposure]. ProRec-Video actively exposes planned transition content, but its simulation/logging policy and propensities are [uncertain].
main_findings_and_limits: RepeatNet and the NBR Reality Check show why overall accuracy can be driven by copying/repetition and why repeat/explore metrics are necessary, but neither turns explore items into semantic new interests. DIEN demonstrates that target-aware temporal interest states improve CTR and reports a 20.7% online CTR lift, but it is not a future-interest classifier. ISLF improves next-click ranking by combining shift and latent factors, yet session IDs and next-item labels cannot establish enduring new interest. CFPRec improves next-POI prediction by inferring future preference representations, but the 'future' is model-imputed, not a supervised future semantic-interest sequence. Distribution-shift work and TGB-Seq are useful low-repeat/future-shift stress tests, not novel-interest benchmarks; TGB-Seq edges lack a stable interest taxonomy. NNBR is the cleanest observed-future novelty task but only for new items. ProRec-Video is closest to multi-step semantic cultivation, yet reliance on agent simulation and unverified datasets/labels prevents treating its reported transition rate as real-world sustained adoption [uncertain].
scale: ISLF reports 375,073/5,969,416/719,470 train sequences and 55,898/55,898/60,858 test sequences for YOOCHOOSE-1/64, YOOCHOOSE-1/4, and Diginetica. CFPRec's three datasets include the paper's PHO split with 2,946 users, 7,247 POIs, and 47,980 check-ins; the other two exact statistics were not re-extracted [uncertain]. NNBR processed statistics are Ta-Feng 13,858 users/11,997 items, dunnhumby 22,530/3,920, and Instacart 19,435/13,897. DIEN industrial scale, distribution-shift data scale, structured-intent scale, and proactive-paper scales are [uncertain]. ProRec-Video says two datasets but gives no accessible abstract counts [uncertain].
stable_user_identity: DIEN uses persistent behavior sequences in public/private CTR data. ISLF's YOOCHOOSE and Diginetica units are anonymous sessions, not durable users. Structured-intent models may use user sequences but do not require cross-domain identity. CFPRec uses persistent check-in users. NNBR uses persistent grocery users/households. ProRec-Video appears user-specific through receptivity profiling, but identity duration is [uncertain].
timestamps_and_order: All verified classical methods consume ordered sequences, but only some preserve absolute time. ISLF splits within sessions and primarily uses order. CFPRec uses ordered daily check-ins and periodicity. NNBR uses basket order. The distribution-shift work explicitly contrasts historical training and future serving distributions. ProRec-Video uses dynamic feedback order, but timestamp resolution and observation duration are [uncertain].
left_censoring_and_history_coverage: Every observational formulation can mistake pre-dataset interests for new ones. This is especially severe for anonymous ISLF sessions, short CTR histories, and finite POI traces. NNBR correctly means unseen in observed baskets only. ProRec-Video's 'beyond historical preferences' also depends on a private or unreported lookback window. None proves lifetime novelty.
item_semantics: DIEN and ISLF can operate on item IDs/features; their latent interests have no auditable semantic taxonomy. Structured-intent states are learned latent variables, not necessarily named categories. CFPRec items are POIs with spatial/context signals; category use in the target is not established here [uncertain]. NNBR primarily uses grocery item IDs. ProRec-Video explicitly uses a hierarchical semantic interest space and video sequences, but the taxonomy, node labels, and mapping release are [uncertain].
feedback_and_exposure: DIEN: impression-conditioned clicks/CTR. ISLF: session clicks. Structured-intent: sequence interactions. CFPRec: POI check-ins. Distribution-shift: future interactions. NNBR: purchases grouped into baskets. Proactive-causal work: intervention responses [uncertain]. ProRec-Video: dynamic feedback, simulated agents, transition-success and satisfaction outcomes [uncertain exact schema].
candidate_space: DIEN scores supplied candidate ads/items. ISLF removes items absent from training and ranks the fixed item vocabulary. Structured-intent and CFPRec rank known items/POIs. NNBR ranks processed novel items without reconstructing true exposure. The distribution-shift benchmark uses sampled/full catalog candidates depending on its experiments [uncertain]. ProRec-Video generates/plans semantic transitions and video sequences, but contemporaneous catalog, retrieval recall, and inventory constraints are [uncertain].
taxonomy_and_opportunity_drift: DIEN/ISLF latent states avoid explicit taxonomy but therefore cannot certify new categories. CFPRec is confounded by POI geography, opening hours, and travel opportunity. NNBR does not reconstruct historical inventory or item launch times. Distribution-shift work highlights popularity/preference drift but does not solve taxonomy drift. ProRec-Video needs versioned interest hierarchy, video-to-interest mapping, item availability, and exposure opportunity; these were not verified [uncertain].
construct_h_f_ynew: DIEN: H(u) is behavior history and F(u) may be future clicks, but the trained target is click probability for a candidate; Y_new is not defined. ISLF: H is a session prefix and F is the next click, but there is no stable user or semantic taxonomy, so category Y_new is not defensible. Structured-intent/CFPRec: H and next event can be formed, but latent intent/future preference is not an observed Y_new. Distribution-shift data may support H/F backtests if raw timestamps and semantics are present, but the paper itself does not define set difference. NNBR exactly supports item-level H=all prior basket items, F=next basket, Y_new=F-H. ProRec-Video could support semantic H/F only if real feedback and the hierarchy are released; currently not reconstructable [uncertain].
leakage_and_missingness_risks: Risks include target-conditioned representations being mistaken for forecasting, model-imputed future preferences being treated as labels, anonymous-session identity leakage, test-vocabulary filtering, missing impressions, sampled negatives, pre-dataset interests, future popularity/catalog leakage, geographic opportunity, and simulated-agent circularity. Proactive paths evaluated by an LLM/agent similar to the generator risk self-confirming transition success [uncertain].
recommended_role: Primary adjacent label-construction reference: NNBR. Required evaluation references: NBR Reality Check and RepeatNet's repeat/explore gate. High-value negative controls and representation baselines: DIEN, ISLF, and structured-intent models, explicitly labeled as CTR/next-item rather than novel-interest prediction. Robustness benchmarks: sequential recommendation under distribution shifts and TGB-Seq, with TGB-Seq treated as method-only because destinations are not interest categories. Auxiliary planning method: CFPRec. Research-direction/method inspiration: proactive causal T-PRA and ProRec-Video, pending real-user data, taxonomy, and persistence validation.
priority: High: NNBR, NBR Reality Check, repeat/explore decomposition, TGB-Seq/distribution-shift stress testing, and ProRec-Video. Medium: proactive causal T-PRA and CFPRec. Low as direct prior work but useful baselines: RepeatNet, DIEN, ISLF, and structured-intent next-item recommendation.
verification_status: Primary abstracts and bibliographic identities were verified for all named works. Full primary PDF/schema facts were verified for ISLF, CFPRec, UpliftRec-related context, and NNBR. DIEN's abstract and online CTR claim are publisher-verified. ProRec-Video title, abstract, headline rates, and DOI are publisher-verified, but its full datasets, taxonomy, simulation protocol, code, and public availability are [uncertain]. The 2025 proactive-causal paper's identity/DOI is verified, while method/data details remain [uncertain].
repeat_explore_and_persistence_audit: RepeatNet explicitly routes repeat versus explore next-item generation, and the NBR Reality Check separately measures repetition/exploration ratios and performance; both are essential evaluation precedents. NNBR goes further by excluding every previously purchased item. DIEN, ISLF, structured-intent, CFPRec, distribution-shift results, and TGB-Seq link MRR can still be dominated by familiar-node structure unless re-evaluated with an explicit contingency table. ProRec-Video is semantically exploratory but does not publicly demonstrate later repeat adoption. CrossInterest should report repeat item, new item in known category, new category, return-after-inactivity, and persistent-new-category outcomes separately.
evidence_quotes_or_schema_facts: DIEN's publisher abstract states that it predicts CTR for a target item and that the evolution layer is target-item-relative. ISLF's PDF defines each label as the next-click item and removes test items absent from training; its datasets are YOOCHOOSE and Diginetica. CFPRec's abstract says multi-step future preferences are inferred from learned past preference to improve next-POI prediction, so they are not observed labels. The distribution-shift paper states that train history and future serving data violate the IID assumption as popularity and preferences evolve. NNBR defines explore items as items not consumed before. ProRec-Video's publisher abstract describes receptivity profiling, hierarchical transition planning, dynamic feedback adaptation, two-dataset evaluation, 85% transition success, and 78.3% satisfaction.
